title: Definition
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: A single hat function $p_a$ can be realized by a neural network with an architecture $(d,2d,1)$. Additionally, after setting $x=(x_1,...,x_d)$, the ordered set of hat functions $P(x) = (p_1(x),...p_{d+1}(x))$ (we will from now on index the order rather than the center $a$) can be realized by a neural network architecture $(d,2d(d+1),d+1)$ or $(d,3d+2,d+1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of this is constructive. The absolute value in $p_k(x)$ on each coordinate $x_k$ can also be written as $|x_k-a_k|=\max(0,x_k-a_k)+\max(0,a_k-x_k)$. This corresponds to two ReLU neurons with weights $\{1,-1\}$ and biases $\{-a_k,a_k\}$. This pattern repeats $d$ times, once for every input coordinate. After setting all weights from the second to the third layer to $-1$ and setting the bias of the last neuron to 1 one gets the same expression as the definition of $p_k(x)$. Since there are $d$ input dimensions and 2 neurons are required to express the absolute value, there need to be $2d$ neurons in the second layer. Therefore the network will have $(d,2d,1)$ architecture.

    The construction of $P(x)$ follows simply from stacking $d+1$ subnetworks that realize different hat functions $p_k(x)$. Since the input space is shared, the architecture becomes $(d,2d(d+1),d+1)$. A visual intuition for the proof is given in Figure \ref{fig:construction}.

    For the $(d,3d+2,d+1)$ bound, let $a_{k,l}$ be the $l$-th entry of the $k$-th center. Then $|x_l-a_{k,l}| = 2\max(0,x_l-a_{k,l})-x_l+a_{k,l}$ and $\sum x_l = \max(0, \sum x_l)+\max(0,-\sum x_l)$. So we write $2\sum_l \max(0,x_l-a_{k,l})-\max(0, \sum_l x_k)+\max(0,-\sum_l x_k)+\sum_l a_{k,l}=\sum_l|x_l-a_{k,l}|$. From this we have an expression for each of the $d+1$ functions in terms of ReLU activations. The constructed centers have three values $\{0,\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2d}\}$, so we need $3d$ neurons realizing them the extra two terms $\max(0,\sum x_l)$ and $\max(0, -\sum x_l)$ add two more neurons to the width giving the architecture $(d,3d+2,d+1)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given an ordered set of hat functions $P = (p_1,p_2,...,p_{d+1})$ with supports $\{U_1,...,U_{d+1}\}$, we will say that $\Omega = \bigcup\limits_{k=1}^{d+1}U_k$ is in a \textit{Helly-arrangement} if $\bigcap\limits_{k=1}^{d+1}U_k \neq \emptyset$.
head: environment

label: Helly construction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Helly construction}
    The open cover $\Omega= \bigcup\limits_{k=1}^{d+1} U_k$ generated by the supports of $d+1$ hat functions with centers $a_k=\frac{1}{2}e_k$ (where $e_k$ is the standard basis) for $k\neq d+1$ and $a_{d+1} = -\frac{1}{2d}\sum_le_l$ forms a Helly-arrangement.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We only need to confirm that the maximal intersection is not empty. If we plug the zero vector into the collection of hat functions $P$, we get $p_i(0) = \max(0,1-\sum|0-\frac{1}{2}e_i|)=\frac{1}{2}$ for all $i<d+1$ and $p_{d+1}(0) = \max(0,1-d/{2d}) = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore the zero vector is in the support of all the functions and the maximal intersection is non-empty.
head: environment

label: semilattice lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{semilattice lemma}
    Given a cover of $\Omega$ defined by the supports of $P$, the intersections can be expressed as $\bigcap\limits_{j\in J} P(U_j) = P(\bigcap\limits_{j\in J} U_j)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: nerve homotopy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{nerve homotopy}
    Given a good cover in Helly arrangement $\Omega = \bigcup\limits_{k=1}^{d+1}U_k$ and a map $P:\Omega\to P(\Omega)$ such that $\bigcap\limits_{j\in J} P(U_j) = P(\bigcap\limits_{j\in J} U_j)$, there is an isomorphism between $N(\Omega)$ and $N(P(\Omega))$ as sets.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This amounts to showing that $J\in N(\Omega) \iff J\in N(P(\Omega))$.

    The first direction is straightforward, if $J \in N(\Omega)$, then $P(U_J) \neq \emptyset$, as $J$ hat functions are supported on this set.

    For the second direction, $J\in N(P(\Omega))$ implies that $\bigcap\limits_{j\in J} P(U_j) \neq \emptyset$ and by applying Lemma \ref{semilattice lemma} we can write it as $P(\bigcap\limits_{j\in J}U_j)\neq \emptyset$, which can only be true if $\bigcap\limits_{j\in J}U_j$ is non-empty. $U_J$ is non-empty for any $J$ since $U_I \subset U_J$ and $U_I\neq \emptyset$.

    Therefore $N(\Omega) \cong N(P(\Omega))$ as sets.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Consider $X=\Omega\cup\partial \Omega$, then $\hat{P}(X)$ has a good cover $C=(\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}\bar{R}_{I\setminus i})\bigcup\bar{V}_I$, where $\bar{R}_J = \{y\in \hat{P}(X): y_j=0 \forall j \notin J\}$ and $\bar{V}_I = \hat{P}(\bar{U}_I)$. This implies that $\hat{P}(X) \cong S^d$ and therefore $\tilde{H}_*(\hat{P}(X)) \cong \tilde{H}_*(S^d)$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textit{sketch:}
\\
The full proof of this statement can be found in Appendix \ref{Appendix}. The intuition is that since $\Omega$ is starshaped, then $X=\bar{\Omega}$ is homeomorphic to the disk $D^d$, additionally we know that $\hat{P}(\partial \Omega)=0$ glues its boundary to a point. This means that $\hat{P}$ acts similarly to a quotient map on the boundary of $D^d$ which gives $D^d/S^{d-1} \cong S^d$. What remains to be shown is that $\hat{P}$ does not lead to non-homotopic identifications elsewhere on $X$.  

To do that we take proposed cover and prove that all possible intersections of its subsets are contractible. Then by Borsuk's nerve theorem \citep{borsuk1948imbedding} we show that the nerve of this cover has the structure of the boundary of the simplex $\partial \Delta^{d+1}\cong S^d$. This simplex is exactly homotopy equivalent to $S^d$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Define the family of maps $\bm{P} = (\hat{P}_1,...,\hat{P}_m):\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{m(d+1)}$ such that $\hat{P}_k(x) = \hat{P}(x;\hat{A}+v_k\bm{1}^T)$, where $v_k\in 6\mathbb{Z}^d$ is different for all $k$ and $\hat{A}$ is the Helly arrangement defined in Proposition \ref{Helly construction}.
head: environment

label: wedge theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{wedge theorem}
    Given the family of maps $\bm{P} = (\hat{P}_1,...,\hat{P}_m)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^d$, we have $\tilde{H}_n(\bm{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)) \cong \tilde{H}_n(\bigvee\limits^{m} S^d)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: thm: wedge sum networks
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: wedge sum networks}
    A neural network of architecture $(d,\sum\limits_{k=1}^d \beta_k W_k,\sum\limits_{k=1}^d \beta_k(k+1))$ can express a space of Betti numbers $\beta= (0,\beta_1,...,\beta_d)$. Additionally, for this network $\bm{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\simeq\bigvee\limits_{k=1}^d(\bigvee\limits^{\beta_k} S^{k})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Start with the $\beta_d$ full dimensional spheres. Representing each such sphere requires a network of architecture $(d,W_d,d+1)$. We can pick $\hat{P}_1(x)$ to have support over a subset of $[-1.5,1.5]^d$. We can pick the next function $\hat{P}_2(x)$ to have support over a subset $[4.5,7.5]\times[-1.5,1.5]^{d-1}$. We can repeat this for all $\beta_d$ spheres, by picking $\text{supp}( \hat{P}_{i}(x)) \subset [-1.5+6(i-1),1.5+6(i-1)]\times[-1.5,1.5]^{d-1}$ while $i\leq \beta_d$ and since the input space is shared we only need to stack the middle and the last layer of the network. Therefore we get the architecture $(d,\beta_dW_d,\beta_d(d+1))$.

    Next we represent the $\beta_{d-1}$, $d-1$-spheres. Each such sphere requires $(d-1, W_{d-1},d)$ neurons. We have to define their supports such that $\text{supp}(\hat{P}_{\beta_d+i}) \subset[-1.5+6(\beta_d+i-1),1.5+6(\beta_d+i-1)]\times[-1.5,1.5]^{d-2}$. We inductively do this for the spheres of any dimension. Since we know that $\beta_k$ copies of $k$-dimensional spheres are expressed by architectures $(k,\beta_kW_{k},\beta_k(k+1))$. Summing over all dimensions gives us the bound $(d,\sum\limits_{k=1}^d\beta_kW_{k},\sum\limits_{k=1}^d\beta_k(k+1))$.

    Finally, the fact that $\bm{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)\simeq\bigvee\limits_{k=1}^d(\bigvee\limits^{\beta_k} S^{k})$ is essentially a restatement of the result in Theorem \ref{wedge theorem}, but with the inclusion of lower-dimensional spheres. Panel B in Figure \ref{fig:wedge} provides an example of the space $S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2 \vee S^2$, which can be represented by a network with architecture (2,24,10).
head: environment

label: lemma:product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:product}
    Let $\Phi_1:X\to Y$ and $\Phi_2: X'\to Y'$ be maps realized by networks of shape $(a,b,c)$ and $(a',b',c')$ respectively. The product map $\Phi_1\times \Phi_2$ is realized by a network with architecture $(a+a',b+b',c+c')$ and $(\Phi_1\times \Phi_2)(X\times X') = \Phi_1(X)\times \Phi_2(X')$ .
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Simply stack the two networks without connecting them in any way. This corresponds to a block diagonal weight matrix and concatenated biases. Each block acts independently on the input, so applying the function to the product is the same as taking the product of the function applied to $X$ and $X'$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For an arbitrary set of target spaces $(S^{d_1},...,S^{d_N})$ realized by architectures $(d_n,W_{d_n},d_n+1)$, we simply sum each architecture to get the total architecture realizing such a space. This gives $(\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n,\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N W_{d_n},\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n+N)$.

    For $S^1\times S^1$, we have $(1,4,2)$ repeated twice so we get $(2,8,4)$.
head: environment

label: thm: exp scaling
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: exp scaling}
    $\sum_k \beta_k(\mathop{\bigtimes}\limits_{N} S^1)$ can scale exponentially as $2^N$, whereas the corresponding architecture scales linearly as $7N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take the $N$-torus given by $\bigtimes^N S^1 = T^N$, its Poincaré polynomial is given by $(1+x)^N$. The coefficients of such a polynomial are the binomial coefficients $\beta_k = C(N,k)$ and the sum of binomial coefficients is $\sum C(N,k) = 2^N$.

    The corresponding architecture for one circle is $(1,4,2)$ and by Lemma \ref{lemma:product} after stacking $N$ copies of it we get $(N,4N,2N)$ which can realize an $N$-torus. So the number of neurons scales as $7N$ which is linear.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: A neural network of shape $(\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n, \sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N W_{d_n}, \sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + N)$ can express a space with Betti numbers given by the coefficients of the Poincaré polynomials, $\mathcal{P}(\mathop{\bigtimes}\limits_{n} S^{d_n}) = \prod\limits_n(1+x^{d_n})$. Additionally, for this network $\textbf{P}(\mathbb{R}^{\sum d_n}) \cong \mathop{\bigtimes}\limits_{n} S^{d_n}$.
head: environment

title: Remark
head: environment

title: Conjecture
body_md:
Denote hidden neurons by $\{h_1(x),...,h_{d+1}(x)\}$ and output neurons by $\{p_1(x),...,p_{d+1}(x)\}$, the following equations provide a tight upper bound $(d,d+1,d+1)$ on architectures expressing the sphere $S^d$.
    
    \begin{align*}
        &h_i(x) = \max(0,x_i) \quad \mathrm{ for } \quad i\neq (d+1), \\
        & h_{d+1}(x) = \max(0,1-\sum^{d+1}_{i=1} x_i),\\
        &p_i(x) = \max(0, h_i(x)+2(1-\sum_{j=1}^{d+1} h_j(x)).
    \end{align*}

    No architecture of shape $(d,d,d+1)$ can express such a sphere. With this bound, the wedge sum bound becomes $(d,\sum_k^d \beta_k(k+1),\sum_k^d \beta_k(k+1))$ and the product bound becomes $(\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n, \sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + N,\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + N)$.
head: environment

label: Main theorem: good cover
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Main theorem: good cover}
    The cover $C=(\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}\bar{R}_{I\setminus i})\bigcup\bar{V}_I$ is a good cover of $\hat{P}(X)$.
head: environment

label: facts
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first identity comes from the fact that we can write $q_k(x) = 1- \sum\limits_{j\neq k}|x_j|-|x_k|-|x_k-\tfrac{1}{2}|+|x_k| = 1-S-g(x_k)$.

    The second identity is similar namely, $q_{d+1}(x) = 1-\sum_l |x_l+\frac{1}{2d}| = 1+\sum_l|x_l|+\sum_l(|x_l+\frac{1}{2d}|-|x_l|) = 1-S-\sum_l h(x_l)$.

    For the third property, notice that $g(t)$ can be written in piecewise-linear form as,
    \begin{align*}
    g(t) = 
        \begin{cases}
            \tfrac{1}{2} \text{ if } t\leq 0,
            \\
            \tfrac{1}{2}-2t \text{ if } 0<t<\tfrac{1}{2},
            \\
            -\tfrac{1}{2} \text{ if } t\geq \tfrac{1}{2}.
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    Then by the first identity we have $0< q_k(x) = 1-S-g(x_k)\leq \frac{1}{2}-g(x_k)$, so $g(x_k)<\tfrac{1}{2}$ which by the PWL form implies that $x_k>0$.

    The fourth property has two cases, when $k\neq d+1$, we have $p_k(x) = 1-S-g(x_k)\leq 0$ and $1-S-g(x_k)\geq \tfrac{1}{2}-S$ (the maximum of $g(t)$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}$). This implies $0\geq \tfrac{1}{2}-S$ so $S\geq \tfrac{1}{2}$. When $k=d+1$, we have $0\geq 1-S-\sum_lh(x_l)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}-S$ so the same conclusion follows. Combining this with fact 3, implies that $x_k>0$ for every $k\in A(x)$.
head: environment

label: Simplex lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Simplex lemma}
    (Simplex lemma) $\bar{R}_T = \Delta^d$ and $\bar{R}_J = \text{conv}\{0, e_k: k \in J\}=\{y_J\geq 0: \sum\limits_{J}y_k\leq1, \text{ } y_i=0 \text{ } i\notin J\}$. Every such $\bar{R}_J$ is contractible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There are two directions to prove, we begin with $\bar{R}_T\subseteq\Delta^d$. We write the sum $\sum_{k\in T} p_k = \alpha-\alpha S-\sum_{k\in A(x)} g(x_k)$.
    Fact 4 also implies that $x_k>0$ for $k\in A(x)$ and $\sum_{k\in A(x)} x_k \leq S$ is implied by $S$ being a norm. Therefore by using the inequality $g(x_k)\geq\frac{1}{2}-2x_k$ we get,
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{k\in T}p_k(x) \leq \alpha(1-S)-\frac{\alpha}{2}+2S=\frac{\alpha}{2} -(\alpha-2)S.
    \end{equation*}
    Then from the fact that $S(\alpha-2)\geq \tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha-2)$ we get $\sum_{k\in T} p_k(x) \leq\tfrac{\alpha}{2}-(\alpha-2)S\leq \tfrac{\alpha}{2}-\tfrac{(\alpha-2)}{2}=1$ which implies that the image is in the simplex. The bound is trivial when $\alpha\leq 1$.

    For the second direction $\Delta^d\subseteq\bar{R}_T$, let $y\in \Delta^d$ and $\sum_k y_k = \|y_T\|_1=S_P$ because all coordinates of the simplex are non-negative (we also have that $S_P\leq 1$). For each $y$ we have to pick a region in which $P$ is affine and then find an $x$ that realizes that $y$ while keeping $p_{d+1}(x)=y_{d+1}=0$. 

    For $d\geq 3$ take $x_k\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]$, from facts 1 and 2 along with the expansions of $g(x_k)$ and $h(x_k)$ each equation can be written as,
    \begin{align*}
        &q_k(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S+2x_k,
        \\
        &p_{d+1}(x) = \max(0,1-S - \frac{d}{2d})= \max(0,\frac{1}{2}-S)=0.
    \end{align*}

    From solving these equations we get $x_k =\tfrac{1}{2}(y_k+S-\tfrac{1}{2})$ and since $\sum x_k = S\geq\tfrac{1}{2}$ (fact 4 and $p_{d+1}(x)=0$), we can write $2S = S_P+(S-\tfrac{1}{2})d$. After rearranging, we get $S= \frac{(d/2)-S_P}{d-2}$ and therefore,
    \begin{equation*}
        x_k = \frac{1}{2}(y_k+\frac{d/2-S_P}{d-2}-\frac{1}{2}).
    \end{equation*}
    It remains to show that these solutions are in fact in the interval $[0,\tfrac{1}{2}]$. $x_k\geq 0$ follows from $S\geq\tfrac{1}{2}$. For $x_k\leq \tfrac{1}{2}$, we have $y_k +\frac{d/2-S_P}{d-2}\leq\frac{3}{2}$. The worst case scenario is when $y_k=S_P$ and the expression becomes $S_P(d-2)+\frac{d}{2}-S_P\leq\frac{3}{2}d-3$. After simplifying we get $S_P(d-3)\leq (d-3)$ and therefore $S_P\leq 1$ when $d>3$ (for $d=3$ we get 0). Therefore, for any $y=(y_T,0)$ we can construct an $x$ such that $P(x)=y$.

    For $d=2$ we can explicitly guess the solution $x^*=(1-\frac{S_P}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{y_1-y_2}{2})$ when $y_1\geq y_2$. Then we get $x_1=1-\frac{S_P}{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}$ and thus $g(x_1) = -\tfrac{1}{2}$. From $y_1-y_2\in[0,1]$ we get $x_2=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{y_1-y_2}{2}\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$ and $g(x_2) = \frac{1}{2}-2x_2$. Then the equations for $P$ become,

    \begin{align*}
        &p_1(x) = \frac{3}{2}-S \\
        &p_2(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S+2x_2\\
        &p_3(x) = \max(0,1-S) = 0.
    \end{align*}
    Then by symmetry, when $y_2>y_1$, the solutions are given by switching the arguments in $x^*$. 

    For $d=1$ we have $\bar{R}_T=[0,1]$.
    
    Given that we have established both $\bar{R}_T\subseteq \Delta^d$ and $\Delta^d \subseteq\bar{R}_T$, we conclude that $\bar{R}_T=\Delta^d$. Furthermore, we have that $\bar{R}_J=\bar{R}_T\cap \{y_k=0, k\in T\setminus J\}$ are faces of $\Delta^d$. Therefore, any such set is contractible.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The sign vector at a point $x$ is given by a map $\tau:\mathbb{R}^d\to \{W^-,W^+,E^-,E^+\}^d$ with components,

    \begin{align*}
        \tau(x)_j = 
        \begin{cases}
            W^- \text{ if } x_j<-\frac{1}{2d},
            \\
            W^+ \text{ if } -\frac{1}{2d}\leq x_j<0,
            \\
            E^- \text{ if } 0 \leq x_j < \frac{1}{2},
            \\
            E^+ \text{ if } \frac{1}{2}\leq x_j.
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    Then the full sign vector is $\tau(x) \in \{W^-, W^+,E^-,E^+\}^d$, we also define $W=\{W^-, W^+\}$ and $E=\{E^-,E^+\}$. By abuse of notation we will, for example, write $t\in E^-$ to mean $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2})$.
head: environment

label: Lowering lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lowering lemma}
    (Lowering lemma) Given $d+1\in J\subsetneq I$, the simplex $\bar{R}_{J\setminus \{d+1\}}$ (Lemma \ref{Simplex lemma}) is a strong deformation retract of $\bar{R}_J$. Therefore $\bar{R}_J$ is contractible.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: Contractible core lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Contractible core lemma}
    (Contractible core lemma) The core $\bar{V}_I=\hat{P}(\bar{U}_I)$ is contractible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Step 1:} $\bar{U}_I=\{S\leq \frac{1}{2}\}$.
    
    Consider the open set $U_I$ on which all functions $p_k$ are active. We have $U_I=\{S< \frac{1}{2}\}$. If $S< \frac{1}{2}$, then by the triangle inequality we have $\|x-a_k\|_1< S+\|a_k\|_1< 1$, which implies $p_k(x) = 1- \|x-a_k\|>0$. Since $\bar{U}_I$ is the closure of $U_I$, we get $\bar{U}_I=\{S\leq\frac{1}{2}\}$. 
    Conversely, suppose that all $p_k(x)>0$ and $S\geq \frac{1}{2}$. Then from fact 3 we get $x_k>0$. This implies that $h(x_k)=\frac{1}{2d}$, so $p_{d+1}(x) < \frac{1}{2}-\sum h(x_k) = 0$. This is a contradiction so $\bar{U} = \{S\leq \frac{1}{2}\}$. 
    
    It is convenient to rewrite the equations again given that $x_k\leq \frac{1}{2}$ (which follows from $S\leq \frac{1}{2}$). \footnote{Notice that since all functions are active we can freely write $p_k(x) = q_k(x)$.} Define $t^\pm=\max(\pm t,0)$, then we get the expressions,

    \begin{align}
    \label{eq: other formulation}
        p_k(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S+2x^+_k \quad (k\in T), \quad p_{d+1}(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S + 2\sum \min(x_l^-,\frac{1}{2d}).
    \end{align}

    \textbf{Step 2:} $\bar{U}_I$ contracts to $a_{d+1}$ and this factors through $\hat{P}$.
    
    We now proceed to prove the contractibility of $\bar{V}_I$ by first constructing a contraction $x(t)$ in the domain $\bar{U}_I$ and then showing that $(x,t)\to \hat{P}(x(t))$ factors through the image map $\hat{P}\times \mathrm{id}$, which is equivalent to requiring that $\hat{P}(x) = \hat{P}(x')$ implies $\hat{P}(x(t)) = \hat{P}(x'(t))$.

    Take the contraction to $a_{d+1}$ given by $x(t) = (1-t)x+ta_{d+1}$. This is a contraction of $\bar{U}_I$ since $a_{d+1}\in \bar{U}_I$, that set is convex and makes $p_{d+1}(x(t))$ linear in $t$ from the equality,
    \begin{align*}
        p_{d+1}(x(t)) &= 1- \|(1-t)x+ta_{d+1}-a_{d+1}\|_1 \\
        &=1-(1-t)\|x-a_{d+1}\|_1\\
        &=1-(1-t)(1-y_{d+1})=p_{d+1}(x'(t)).
    \end{align*}

    This property does not hold for the other functions $p_k(x)=y_k$, so instead we show that they are determined by $y$. Use the equality $\hat{P}(x) = \hat{P}(x')$ and equation \ref{eq: other formulation} to express,
    \begin{align*}
        p_k(x) &= \frac{1}{2}-\|x\|_1+2x_k^+\\
        &=\frac{1}{2}-\|x'\|_1+2{x'}_k^+=p_k(x')
    \end{align*}
    By rearranging the individual terms we get $p_k(x)-(\frac{1}{2}-S)=2x_k^+\geq 0$ and $p_{d+1}(x) -(\frac{1}{2}-S) = 2\sum \min(x^-_l,\frac{1}{2d})\geq 0$. This implies that at least one $p_i(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S$, since either $x_k\leq0$ for some $k$ and thus $p_k(x)-(\frac{1}{2}-S) = 0$ implying $p_k(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S$ or $x>0$ implying $x_l^-=0$ and $p_{d+1}(x) = \frac{1}{2}-S$ and $\min_i(y_i)\leq \frac{1}{2}-S$. We also have $\min_i(y_i)\geq \frac{1}{2}-S$ from the fact that the formulas in \ref{eq: other formulation} add a positive term to $\frac{1}{2}-S$. Therefore, $S = \frac{1}{2}-\min_i(y_i)$ only depends on $y$, so $S=\|x\|_1=\|x'\|_1$ and $x_k^+={x'}_k^+$.

    It remains to show that $\|x(t)\|_1=\|x'(t)\|_1$ and $x(t)^+=x'(t)^+$. We can define the set where $x$ and $x'$ have non-positive values as $Z = \{l:x_l\leq 0\} = \{l: {x'}_l\leq 0\}$. Off this set we have $x_l(t)=x'_l(t)$. On this set we have, $\max((1-t)x-\frac{t}{2d},0)=x(t)^+=x'(t)^+=0$ and $|x_l(t)| = (1-t)|x_l|+\frac{t}{2d}$. In other words, the different preimages of $y$ only differ only in coordinates in $Z$. Then summing over $N$ gives $\sum_{l\in Z}|x_l(t)| = (1-t)\sum_{l\in Z}|x_l|+\frac{t|Z|}{2d} = \sum_{l\in Z}|x_l'(t)|$, with the last equality coming from the fact that $Z$ is the same for both points. Thus, we get that off $Z$ the coordinates agree and on $Z$ the sums of the absolute values agree, this implies $\|x(t)\|_1=\|x'(t)\|_1$ and $x(t)^+=x'(t)^+$. From this we see that $\hat{P}(x) = \hat{P}(x')$ implies $\hat{P}(x(t)) = \hat{P}(x'(t))$.

    \textbf{Step 3:} $\bar{V}_I$ is contractible.
    
    From the previous step we concluded that $\hat{P}(x(t))= y(t)$ is independent of the choice of the starting point $x(0)\in \bar{U}_I$ with $P(x(0))=y$. Another way to state this property is to say that the map $F(x,t)=\hat{P}(x(t))$ factors through $\hat{P}\times \mathrm{id}$, meaning that the following diagram commutes,
    \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
      \bar U_I\times[0,1] \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\hat{P}\times\mathrm{id}"'] & \bar V_I \\
      \bar V_I\times[0,1] \arrow[ur, dashed, "\Phi"']
    \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    $\hat{P}$ is continuous, $\bar{U}\times[0,1]$ is compact and $P\times \mathrm{id}$ is a continuous surjection (simply because $\bar{V}_I=\hat{P}(\bar{U}_I)$) onto a Hausdorff space. Thus it is closed and a quotient map. $F(x,t) = \hat{P}(x(t))= \Phi\circ P\times\mathrm{id}$ is also continuous due to the continuity of $\hat{P}$, so $\Phi$ is continuous. This allows us to write the retraction on the image space $\bar{V}\times [0,1]$ as $\Phi(\hat{P}(x),t)$. We then have $\Phi(\hat{P}(x),0) = \hat{P}(x)$ because $x(0)=x$ and $\Phi(\hat{P}(x),1) = e_{d+1}$ because $x(1) = a_{d+1}$ and $\hat{P}(a_{d+1}) = e_{d+1}$. Thus $\Phi$ is a homotopy starting from the identity and ending at the constant map with value $e_{d+1}$. Therefore the identity is null-homotopic and $\bar{V}_I$ is contractible.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Contractible intersection lemma}
    (Contractible intersection lemma) For $\emptyset \neq J\subsetneq I$, the intersections $\bar{R}_J\cap\bar{V}_I$ are contractible.

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof consists in showing that every intersection of the cover is contractible, which we have done in the previous four lemmas. Here we simply list them.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Intersections of the type $\bar{R}_J$ with $d+1\notin J$ are simplices by Lemma \ref{Simplex lemma}.
        \item Intersections of the type $\bar{R}_J$ with $d+1\in J\neq I$ are (strong) deformation retract to simplices by Lemma \ref{Lowering lemma}.
        \item The core $\bar{V}_I = \hat{P}(\bar{U}_I)$ is contractible by Lemma \ref{Contractible core lemma}.
        \item Intersections of the type $\bar{V}_I\cap\bar{R}_J$, with $\emptyset \neq J\subsetneq I$ contract to simplices when $d+1\notin J$ or to a graph over simplices when $d+1\in J$ by Lemma \ref{Contractible intersection lemma}.
    \end{enumerate}
    Given that all this list exhausts all possible intersections, $C$ is a good cover of $\hat{P}(X)$.

title: Theorem
body_md: $N(C)$ is homotopy equivalent to the sphere $S^d$.

title: Proof
body_md: This simply follows by looking at the intersection pattern of all pieces of the cover. The conditions $\bar{R}_K\cap\bar{R}_J = \bar{R}_{K\cap J}$ along with the intersections $\bar{V}_I\cap \bar{R}_J \neq \emptyset$ imply that the nerve $N(C)$ contains every proper subset of the $d+2$ possible vertices. The only special intersections are the one including all closed strata $\bigcap (R_{I\setminus i}) = \textbf{0}$ and its intersection with the core $\textbf{0}\cap \bar{V}_I = \emptyset$. Therefore, the nerve has $d+2$ vertices which realize all intersections except for the $d+1$ face. This is equivalent to taking the boundary $\partial\Delta^{d+1}$, which is homotopy equivalent to $S^d$.
